title: Androgenetic alopecia (male/female pattern baldness): polygenic inheritance with variable expressivity
vignette: A 32-year-old woman comes to the office due to worry that she will go bald. Her father had a receding hairline with apical baldness beginning at age 20 and was completely bald by age 35. The patient's paternal grandmother and multiple other relatives on her paternal side also had early-onset baldness, but her father's siblings and the maternal side of her family have had no problems with unusual hair loss. Physical examination shows mild thinning of hair at the temporal areas, with an otherwise normal hairline, thickness, and coloration. There is no excess hair growth on her face or trunk, and she has a normal female pattern of pubic hair growth. Palpation of the thyroid is normal. Which of the following is the most likely inheritance pattern of the hair loss in this patient's family?

clues.text: apical baldness beginning at age 20 and was completely bald by age 35
clues.note: Early-onset patterned baldness (temporal/vertex) is androgenetic alopecia - the most common cause of hair loss in men and women.

clues.text: mild thinning of hair at the temporal areas
clues.note: Temporal/vertex patterned thinning driven by androgens and genetics is characteristic of androgenetic alopecia.

whatMatters: ANDROGENETIC ALOPECIA (patterned baldness) is driven by BOTH hormonal (androgens) and GENETIC factors and demonstrates POLYGENIC inheritance with variable expressivity (multiple loci, including on chromosome 20 and the androgen-receptor gene). Answer D.
strategy: Recognize androgenetic alopecia and recall it is POLYGENIC (multiple genes + hormonal influence, variable expressivity). The family pattern isn't a clean single-gene ratio. Reject single-gene patterns: autosomal dominant (not a clean vertical dominant trait), autosomal recessive (would show ~25% of offspring from carriers, not seen), mitochondrial (maternal transmission, all offspring affected - here it's paternal), and sporadic (there is clear familial clustering).

eliminations.label: Autosomal dominant - not a single dominant gene
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a single-gene trait transmitted vertically with ~50% risk. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: androgenetic alopecia results from MULTIPLE genes plus hormonal effects (some loci are X-linked, others autosomal), not one dominant gene. ✅ Correct if: a Mendelian dominant condition with a clean pedigree.

eliminations.label: Autosomal recessive - no 25% carrier pattern
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: disease in ~25% of offspring from two asymptomatic carriers, typically skipping generations. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the pedigree shows dominant-appearing familial clustering across generations, not a recessive pattern. ✅ Correct if: consanguinity/carrier parents with affected offspring.

eliminations.label: Mitochondrial - maternal transmission
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: exclusively MATERNAL inheritance with all offspring affected. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the baldness is transmitted through the PATERNAL side here; mitochondrial inheritance would follow the mother. ✅ Correct if: maternally transmitted trait affecting all children.

eliminations.label: Sporadic - clear family clustering present
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: haphazard occurrence without an inheritance pattern (e.g., a de novo mutation). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: multiple affected relatives on the paternal side indicate a heritable (familial) pattern, not sporadic. ✅ Correct if: an isolated case with no family history.

reasoning: The patterned, early-onset baldness is androgenetic alopecia
Androgenetic alopecia is influenced by multiple genes plus androgens (variable expressivity)
This does not fit a single-gene (dominant/recessive/mitochondrial) pattern
mechanism: ANDROGENETIC ALOPECIA (male- and female-pattern baldness) is the MOST COMMON cause of hair loss in both sexes. As the name implies, it depends on BOTH HORMONAL (circulating ANDROGENS acting via the androgen receptor and 5-alpha-reductase/dihydrotestosterone) and GENETIC factors, with hair loss concentrated at the TEMPORAL areas and VERTEX and progressing over life; pattern and severity vary between individuals and sexes. Its inheritance is POLYGENIC with VARIABLE EXPRESSIVITY: many susceptibility loci contribute, including a major locus on the short arm of chromosome 20 and variation in the ANDROGEN-RECEPTOR gene on the X chromosome (so some genetic factors are X-linked while others are autosomal). Because MULTIPLE genes plus hormonal influences combine - rather than a single Mendelian gene - it does not follow a clean dominant, recessive, or mitochondrial pattern, and the strong familial clustering excludes 'sporadic.' Hence the inheritance is POLYGENIC. (Other polygenic/multifactorial conditions include hypertension, type 2 diabetes, ischemic heart disease, glaucoma, epilepsy, and schizophrenia.)

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Genetics > polygenic/multifactorial traits: androgenetic alopecia, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, ischemic heart disease, schizophrenia, epilepsy, glaucoma; androgenetic alopecia = androgen + multiple genes (chr 20, androgen-receptor gene), variable expressivity.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Patterned baldness = androgenetic alopecia = polygenic (multiple genes + hormones), variable expressivity.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on polygenic/multifactorial inheritance, variable expressivity, androgenetic alopecia, or single-gene vs polygenic? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: AD/AR/mitochondrial are single-gene patterns; sporadic ignores the clear family clustering.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: androgenetic alopecia = polygenic with variable expressivity (androgens + multiple loci); a classic multifactorial trait.

memoryHook: Pattern baldness runs in families but not by one clean gene - it's a team effort of many genes plus hormones: polygenic.
